curves-crossing-s1.title: A market graph with a shaded triangle and rectangle

items.q: What is true at the point where two curves on a graph cross?
options: The two curves have the same slope there
The price is at its highest value on the graph
The point lies on both curves, so both share its price and quantity
The quantity is 0

why.correct: An intersection is the one point that sits on both curves at once, so both curves give the same price and quantity there.
options: A downward curve and an upward curve have opposite slopes, even where they cross.
The crossing point can be at any height.
Right: one point, on both curves.
The crossing point usually sits well away from the vertical axis.

items.q: In the graph, at what price and quantity do D and S cross?
options: \$5 and 50 boxes
\$10 and 0 boxes
\$5 and 100 boxes
\$50 and 5 boxes

why.correct: Follow the dashed lines from E: across to \$5 on the price axis and down to 50 boxes on the quantity axis.
options: Right: E is at (50, \$5).
That is where D meets the price axis, not where D meets S.
100 boxes is where D reaches the quantity axis.
This swaps the values: the quantity is 50 and the price is \$5.

items.q: What is the area of triangle A, which lies under D and above the \$5 price, from 0 to 50 boxes?

why.correct: Base: 50 boxes (from 0 to 50). Height: \$10 - \$5 = \$5. Area $= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 50 \times 5 = 125$. Unit 2 names this triangle consumer surplus.

mistakes.why: That is base times height, the area of a rectangle. A triangle is half of that: ½ × 50 × 5.
The height runs from \$5 up to \$10, which is 5, not 10. Measure from the price line, not from the axis.

items.q: What is the area of rectangle B, under the \$5 price from 0 to 50 boxes?

why.correct: A rectangle's area is base × height: $50 \times 5 = 250$.

mistakes.why: That halves the area, which is the rule for a triangle. B is a rectangle: base × height with no ½.

items.q: If D shifted right and the new crossing point were at \$6 and 60 boxes, how would the new rectangle under the price, out to the quantity, compare with B?
options: It would be smaller, because D moved
It would be the same, 250
It would be larger: 60 × 6 ÷ 2 = 180
It would be larger: 60 × 6 = 360

why.correct: A rectangle under the new price out to the new quantity has base 60 and height 6: $60 \times 6 = 360$, larger than 250.
options: Both the price and the quantity rose, so the rectangle grows.
The base and height both changed, so the area changed.
That halves a rectangle; the ½ belongs only to triangles.
Right: both the base and the height grew.

items.q: More shoppers start coming to the market, so at every price buyers want more boxes of strawberries. Shift the right curve and mark the new crossing point.

why.correct: More buyers shift D right. The new crossing point slides up along S: a higher price and a larger quantity.

slips.S: Shoppers are buyers, so they move D; S would move only if the farmers' costs or numbers changed.

items.q: A late frost damages the strawberry crop, so at every price farmers bring fewer boxes. Shift the right curve and mark the new crossing point.

why.correct: The frost shifts S left. The new crossing point slides up along D: a higher price and a smaller quantity.

key.because: a frost that damages the crop

slips.D: The frost changes what farmers can bring, so it moves S, not the buyers' curve D.

items.q: Shade the triangle that lies under the downward-sloping curve D and above the horizontal line through the crossing point, from 0 out to the crossing quantity.

why.correct: The triangle has the vertical axis on its left, D on top and the horizontal line at the crossing price below, and it ends at the crossing quantity. Unit 2 names this triangle consumer surplus.

slips.ps: That triangle sits BELOW the crossing price and above S. The one asked for sits above the price and under D.

items.q: Shade the triangle that lies above the upward-sloping curve S and below the horizontal line through the crossing point, from 0 out to the crossing quantity.

why.correct: The triangle has the vertical axis on its left, the horizontal line at the crossing price on top and S below, and it ends at the crossing quantity. Unit 2 names this triangle producer surplus.

slips.cs: That triangle sits ABOVE the crossing price and under D. The one asked for sits below the price and above S.

items.q: A triangle on a graph has a base of 30 units along the quantity axis and a height of \$8. What is its area, in dollars?

mistakes.why: That is the rectangle. A triangle with the same base and height is half of it.

items.q: A table shows that at \$2 buyers want 70 bags and sellers offer 30; at \$3, 60 and 45; at \$4, 50 and 50; at \$5, 40 and 55. At what price do the two curves cross?

why.correct: The curves cross where both give the same quantity. At \$4 buyers want 50 bags and sellers offer 50.
options: At \$2 buyers want 70 but sellers offer only 30.
Right: 50 wanted and 50 offered.
At \$5 sellers offer 55 but buyers want only 40.
At \$3 buyers want 60 but sellers offer 45.

items.q: The buyers' curve D shifts right and the sellers' curve S stays put. Along which curve does the crossing point move?
options: Along D, the curve that moved
Along S, the curve that did not move
Along neither: it stays where it was
Down the vertical axis

why.correct: The new crossing point must lie on both the new D and the old S. S did not move, so the point slides along S.
options: The old D is gone; the new point is on the new D and on S, so it moves along S.
Right: it stays on the curve that held still.
A shift moves the crossing point to a new place.
Crossing points sit where the curves meet, not on an axis.

items.q: Put the steps for finding the area of a triangle on a graph in order.
options: Find the triangle's corners on the graph
Read its base along the horizontal axis
Read its height along the vertical axis
Multiply ½ × base × height

why.correct: Locate the shape, read the base and the height from its own edges, then apply the formula.
